correctness.rationale: Exact-multiplicity lower bound is forced by constant patterns after deletion; \(k+1\) permutation blocks suffice. For \(k\ge2\), deleting the last b forces \(a_i<b_{i+1}\) for \(1\le i<k\), and deleting the first a forces the \(i=k\) inequality via pattern \(a^{k-1}b\). All \(i\)-th symbol occurrences thus precede all \((i+1)\)-st occurrences. This proves structural necessity and factorial counting, with \(k=1\) handled separately. Independent literal enumeration of 413244 multiset hosts across 11 parameter pairs matches without using these inequalities.

evidence: Barker et al. 2020 give arch factorization and ordinary/circular universality properties.
Adamson et al. 2023 provide general regular-language k-universality counting algorithms, not the minimum one-erasure-host enumeration.
The new theorem gives a specific if-and-only-if characterization at length \(q(k+1)\), not just effective computability.
broader_coverage.reasoning: A general algorithm might be specialized to test the property, and known permutation-block enumeration counts ordinary \((k+1)\)-universal shortest words. Neither mathematically implies the asserted equivalence with one-deletion robustness without the new necessary occurrence-order inequalities.

evidence: The 2021 deletion-distance algorithm starts with a given word and index; no explicit classification of \(q(k+1)\)-length words meeting a universal single-deletion predicate occurs in its inspected theorem and extension material.
The 2023 counting algorithms do not identify robust minimizers from k+1 universality or distinguish \(k=1\).
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Published results supply definitions and general algorithms but not the all-parameter sharp criterion. In particular, the \(k=1\) exception shows that a naive blanket equivalence to \((k+1)\)-universality would be false. The new proof directly characterizes a condition that algorithms can check but do not resolve symbolically.

evidence: Day et al. STACS 2021 Theorem 4.4 computes minimal deletion distance to achieve an index; the full inspected theorem contains no quantification over all single deletions of all minimum-length hosts.
Adamson 2023 ranks and counts ordinary k-universal words, and identifies the ordinary k-universal language, without one-deletion resilience classification.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The event every one-position deletion preserves k-universality is equivalent to deletion distance at least two to the complement of k-universal words, not the distance from a given word to the k-universal language. An algorithm for general membership/counting does not by itself assert the explicit optimal-host equivalence and exceptional \(k=1\) count.

originality.rationale: Targeted primary full-text and mathematical-record comparisons did not identify the exact minimum-length one-deletion-resilience classification; the strongest related prior theorem computes deletion distance to a specified universality index, but does not characterize and enumerate all minimum-length hosts resilient to every individual deletion. This distinction is mathematical rather than titular: the new theorem proves robustness implies the strictly stronger \((k+1)\)-universality exactly at the optimum length for \(k\ge2\), with a sharp \(k=1\) exception.
residual_risks: An unindexed prior equivalence or a specialization embedded in a broader theorem may exist.
The novelty comparison rests on inspected relevant sections and mathematical-record coverage, not an exhaustive search of all mathematics literature.

value.rationale: The smallest redundancy needed to retain complete subsequence coverage after an arbitrary erasure is a natural coding/string-design invariant. The theorem determines this threshold for every alphabet and pattern length, proves surprising permutation-block rigidity for \(k\ge2\), exhibits a nontrivial exceptional \(k=1\) boundary, and enumerates every optimum. It is an all-parameter structural classification, not merely a small census.
